source.title: PPE-Bench: A Benchmark for Evaluating MLLM Unlearning under Private-Public Entanglement
source.authors: Xianren Zhang; Delvin Ce Zhang; Dongwon Lee; Su-Hang Wang

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether fine-tuning after multimodal unlearning restores forgotten private information, a conceptual test of recovery using a different setting and data than the claim’s language-model examples.
record.gate_note: The paper tests recovery by fine-tuning on public information and reports unlearning and retain-set performance. It does not test activation-direction ablation, quantization, or prompt-only recovery. The plotted values for relearning and retain-set performance are not numerically transcribed in the text; these rows use figure-only values and the authors’ stated descriptions. Table 2’s additional inpainting comparison and Figure 3’s adjacent-public-information results are not separately recorded here.
record.test_reason: The paper applies standard unlearning methods (GA, NPO, KL-Min, GD) to multimodal LLMs. It then fine-tunes the unlearned models on benign public-entity questions over retain-set images and measures forget-set accuracy again (Sec 4.5, Fig 5). That is a direct test of recovery by fine-tuning (B), and of A's robustness half, in a new multimodal, visually entangled setting. Forget-set and retain-set results also bear on A's effectiveness and utility parts.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also introduce PIP and target-guided blurring, which preserve public info at some cost to forgetting. They interpret relearning recovery as showing that methods suppress rather than erase private information.
record.recipe_differences: Uses multimodal unlearning on synthetic private-person/public-entity image data, then fine-tunes on public-information questions; this is not a direct replication of the original text-model settings.
record.method_sensitivity: Seen versus unseen images change forget-set accuracy; the paper reports that PIP preservation can weaken forgetting. Relearning outcomes are stated for standard methods, while PIP starts with higher forget accuracy.
record.peer_reviewed: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
record.problems: The dataset uses fictitious individuals and generated images; the authors note that the benchmark covers only one target individual, one public figure, and one landmark per image. Retain-set and relearning results are presented in plots without numerical values in the text; no uncertainty estimates are stated.
record.rows_left_out: Figure 3 adjacent-public-information accuracy results and Table 2’s inpainting comparison (including forget and public-information accuracy) are not recorded as separate rows. The retained rows prioritize the core forget-accuracy tests, reported relearning results, and retain-set utility; plotted values not stated in text remain figure only.

untested.parts: No chance-level threshold is given. Attacks other than benign fine-tuning are not tested. Relearning is shown for one model only.
Size of the relearning set is not varied. No relearning on a subset of the forgotten facts. No numeric recovery values in the text. No LLaVA relearning. PIP recovery is not reported.
Not tested. The authors infer suppression rather than erasure from relearning alone, with no internal analysis.
PIP and blurring are aimed at preserving public info, not at resisting attacks. Blurring still shows recovery.

missing.what: Adjacent public-information accuracy after unlearning on Qwen: vanilla 98.0 vs GA 30.4, NPO 35.3, KL-Min 3.8, GD 13.7, PIP 81.3/79.2, blurring 80.1. Bears on A's 'keeps general ability'.
Numeric before/after forget accuracy for relearning, and which model was used.
Inpainting variant: forget 9.1%, public 85.3%. Also, Table 2 gives GA forget as 10.3 while Table 1 gives 13.7, an internal inconsistency.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's B limits_scope label for PIP was dropped: the PIP relearning rows are cannot_determine, so they cannot qualify the version. Tranche changed from T2 to T3, because this is a new multimodal setting tested with the same relearning question. Relearning evidence is figure-only and unquantified in the text.

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not establish a chance-level threshold for targeted accuracy. It does not test internal edits, quantization, or prompt-only attacks.
Tests further fine-tuning on benign public information; does not test a few-shot relearning set, a subset of forgotten facts, or separately varied unrelated versus loosely related examples.
Activation-direction ablation and analysis of access-blocking versus deletion are not tested.
Rephrasing, jailbreaks, other languages, and in-context information are not tested.
No counter-method is tested for resistance to the listed attacks.

source_check.notes: Fig 4 and Fig 5 name no model (the main text uses Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct). Relearning is figure-only and its set size is not stated. Table 2 gives Qwen unseen GA forget 10.3, against 13.7 in Table 1, and shows adjacent public info falling 98.0 -> 30.4/35.3/3.8/13.7 (GA/NPO/KL-Min/GD). PIP and blurring are the authors' own methods. Both models trained with LoRA.

statements.correction: Sec 4.5 / Fig 5: fine-tuning on public-entity questions over retain-set images raises forget accuracy for GA, NPO, KL-Min, GD and blurring. The values are figure-only and the model is not named. Authors: the methods suppress rather than erase. Sec 4.4: GA, NPO and KL-Min clearly drop retain-set accuracy. Table 2 (Qwen, unseen): adjacent public-info accuracy is 98.0 for vanilla, 35.3 for NPO, 13.7 for GD. The examples GD 70.1->0.3 (Qwen) and GA 54.4->3.8 (LLaVA) are seen-image values. NPO/GD range 0.3-4.0 from 41.9-70.1 is correct.
statements.problem: The numbers are right, but the entry reads this study as support for A without saying that the same study's benign fine-tuning brings the forgotten information back for these methods. For this study the conditions line ('only prompt, image, paraphrase and sampling attacks') is wrong. NPO also clearly lowers retain accuracy. The GA example sits under an 'NPO and GD' lead.

statements.correction: LLaVA-1.5-7B GD, unseen images: 41.9 -> 2.3 keyword ACC (Table 4); seen images 54.4 -> 1.7. No chance level given. Both models are trained with LoRA (Table 5).

Fine-tuning on public-information questions over retain-set images raises forget accuracy for GA, NPO, KL-Min, GD and blurring (Sec 4.5, Fig 5; the text gives no numbers). PIP variants are already relatively high before fine-tuning.
statements.problem: Lists PPE-Bench under recovery after small forget-type sets. Its relearning data is benign public-entity questions on retain-set images, not forget-type data. The set size is not stated, recovery is figure-only, and the model is not named.
